newsitem.title: EGYPT: Arabs see victorious Clinton active in Mideast.
newsitem.headline: Arabs see victorious Clinton active in Mideast.

text.p: Arabs predicted on Wednesday that U.S. diplomacy would swing into action in the Middle East after President Bill Clinton's election victory, but few dared ring alarm bells by openly asking Washington to lean on Israel.
"We think that his re-election opens the door for a more active role by the U.S. and we would welcome this," Jordanian Information Minister Marwan Muasher told Reuters.
"He has been very instrumental in pushing the peace process forward and we hope he will do even more in terms of getting the peace process out of its present crisis," he added.

"His election no doubt gives confidence that this partner will continue the peace process and will do everything possible to narrow the gap between points of views," added Egyptian Information Minister Safwat el-Sherif.

"It is prime time that the U.S. played an active role in the peace talks between Palestinians and Israelis and acts as a referee," the speaker of the Palestinian Legislative Council, Ahmed Korei, told Reuters.

Arab states had shown no preference in public in the U.S. presidential elections while Arab commentators watched with distaste as both candidates appeared to lean over backwards to woo the votes of American Jews.
But if they had to choose, Arab governments would have preferred Clinton, if only to save the time it would have taken Republican Bob Dole to get to grips with Middle East affairs.
U.S. presidential election campaigns are always a frustrating time for Arab leaders, most of whom do not face the same need to fight off domestic challenges to their power.
This year it was especially trying because of the stalemate in peace talks after right-wing Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu took office in June.

In private, Arab leaders would be happy to see the kind of sniping that broke out between Israel and the U.S. administration in the days of U.S. President George Bush and Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Shamir, diplomats say. Few are willing to say so, for fear it would backfire.
Senior Palestinian peace negotiator Hassan Asfour, referring to the Arab grievance that Netanyahu has reneged on old deals, said he hoped Washington would set him right.
"We hope that the U.S. administration will...take the necessary steps to protect peace agreements and find the right means to do so," he told Reuters.
Muasher, the Jordanian minister, went further than most of his Arab colleagues on Wednesday, saying he did expect Clinton to lean harder on the Israeli government.
"In my opinion there's no doubt the U.S. president will put on more pressure than he has in the past," he told the Arabic service of the British Broadcasting Corporation.

"Any president who is elected for a second term has more freedom of manoeuvre and I also believe that the U.S. president has a desire to go down in history as the president who finally solved the Arab-Israeli conflict," he said.
"But we must not rely on such pressure more than necessary because he might come up against interests inside and outside the United States," he added.
The U.S. ambassador to Israel, Martin Indyk, who once described himself as a Zionist, told reporters in Cairo last week that such a scenario was out of the question.
"If the question is whether the United States will come down with a sledgehammer on Israel and deliver concessions -- that's not the way we pursue the peace process," he said.

"We do not believe in imposing peace. In the end it is up to the parties themselves. The leaders in this region have to make critical decisions, they are answerable to their people and they are the ones who must decide," he added.
Netanyahu took the same line in an interview on Israel's Channel One television on Tuesday.

"If he (Palestinian President Yasser Arafat) is waiting for the great pressure that has to come from Washington, he will be disappointed because it will not come. The whole idea that Netanyahu will stand and be whipped by the next president of the United States is simply not serious," he said.
